channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Marine
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] North Carolina Ports fell back to manual gate and cargo processing after a breach of its core IT
item.description: North Carolina Ports confirmed that an outside actor breached its main IT infrastructure on 4–5 August 2026, forcing all three locations — Wilmington, Morehead City and the Charlotte Inland Port — onto manual gate and cargo processing. The US Coast Guard and state agencies were notified. A spokesperson said the breach was contained and the organisation was in recovery; no ransomware group had publicly claimed it at the time of reporting and no data theft has been confirmed. This is an IT-side compromise with operational consequences rather than a control-system attack, which is the dominant shape of port incidents: terminal operating systems, gate automation and cargo documentation are business systems whose failure stops physical movement just as effectively as touching a crane would. - North Carolina Ports — via The Record, BleepingComputer, Splash247 - Incident 4–5 Aug 2026; reported 6 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] A breach at CEVA Logistics rippled out to banks, retailers and gamers across Europe
item.description: An intrusion at CEVA Logistics, part of shipping line CMA CGM’s group, began on 29 July 2026 and was confirmed to customers on 1 August. Names, addresses, phone numbers and emails tied to customer orders were exposed across an unusually varied client list — including Bol, De Bijenkorf, Ajax FC, ING, Ace & Tate and Valve/Steam hardware customers — and shipping was delayed across eight European warehouses. Ten organisations reported the breach to Dutch regulators. For maritime and logistics operators the lesson is downstream blast radius: a third-party logistics provider holds order and consignee data for dozens of unrelated brands, so one compromise becomes many notifications, and the disruption lands on customers who have no contractual relationship with the breached party. - CEVA Logistics customer notification — via TechCrunch - Breach began 29 Jul 2026; reported 10 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Attackers took hands-on control of water-utility PLCs across a dozen states — locking out operators and knocking a treatment plant offline
item.description: Between 26–27 July 2026 a coordinated campaign disrupted automated controls at more than 30 Minnesota community water systems, and confirmed intrusions have since been reported across roughly a dozen states including Georgia, Michigan, South Dakota, Alabama and New Jersey. This is hands-on manipulation of control equipment, not a data breach: CISA says the actors changed PLC passwords and altered device IP addresses to lock operators out of their own equipment. In Braham, Minnesota a pump failure forced a treatment facility offline and prompted a resident conservation notice; Clayton County, Georgia issued a precautionary boil-water advisory after a pump-station disruption, later lifted. Dragos’s Rob Lee told NPR he could not recall “this many targets at once with operational impact.” Every affected utility reported that drinking water stayed safe, with staff falling back to manual operation. Federal officials have pointed to Iran-linked activity — a TLP:AMBER WaterISAC assessment reportedly found the evidence aligned with campaigns previously attributed to Iran — but no formal public attribution has been made, so treat the actor as suspected rather than confirmed. - CISA / FBI / EPA, MNIT and affected city statements — via NPR, The Record, Dark Reading, BleepingComputer - Incidents from 26 Jul 2026; scope reporting through 12 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Cisco ASA and Firepower join KEV under active exploitation — the OT perimeter is the target again
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-20349, a heap-inspection vulnerability in Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and Firepower Threat Defense software, to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 11 August 2026, citing evidence of active exploitation. The same batch added CVE-2026-68820, a use-after-free in the Windows afd.sys driver enabling local privilege escalation — relevant because Windows engineering workstations and HMI servers are exactly where that gets chained after initial access — and CVE-2026-72898, a SQL injection in Metabase exposing stored credentials. Earlier in the month CISA added CVE-2026-8037, an unauthenticated command injection in Progress Kemp LoadMaster carrying CVSS 9.6, after sustained exploitation attempts, with a federal patch deadline of 10 August under BOD 26-04. None of these are ICS products. All of them sit in front of, or inside, the path into OT. - CISA KEV catalogue — via The Hacker News, CyberExperts - KEV additions 3, 4, 7 and 11 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] An N-able N-central auth bypass was exploited, patched incompletely, then exploited again
item.description: CISA added two N-able N-central authentication-bypass flaws to KEV within two days: CVE-2026-18556 and CVE-2026-18577, both CVSS 8.2, the second being an incomplete-fix follow-on to the first. N-able confirmed a limited number of customer breaches. Attackers who exploit it take over administrator accounts and can pivot to managed endpoints through the platform’s Take Control remote-session feature. Huntress reported that 55.6% of reachable cloud servers were still unpatched at the time of its analysis. The fix is 2026.3.1.7 / 2026.3 HF1. RMM platforms matter disproportionately in OT because they are how integrators, machine builders and managed-service providers reach plant equipment — often through a path that was never security-reviewed and does not appear on the network diagram. - CISA KEV; N-able advisory — via The Hacker News, Help Net Security - KEV additions 3–4 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 10.0 command injection in Haiwell’s cloud HMI gateway hands an unauthenticated attacker root
item.description: CISA advisory ICSA-26-225-02 covers CVE-2026-19188, an OS command injection (CWE-78) in the Haiwell IoT Cloud HMI Gateway that scores the full CVSS 10.0. The flaw sits in the device’s Net Check function: an unauthenticated attacker can reach the cmdPing Socket.io event and execute arbitrary commands as root. CISA flags the product’s use in energy, critical manufacturing and water/wastewater environments. Affected firmware is 3.40.1.12; the fix is 3.50.1.19. No in-the-wild exploitation had been reported at publication, which is the good news — a maximum-severity, unauthenticated, internet-reachable root execution on a gateway product is exactly the profile that gets weaponised quickly once someone bothers. - CISA ICSA-26-225-02 - Published 13 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] August ICS Patch Tuesday: a maximum-severity missing-authentication flaw in Siemens Simatic IoT2050, plus Schneider and Phoenix Contact fixes
item.description: Siemens published ten advisories in the August cycle. The headline item is a maximum-severity missing-authentication vulnerability in Simatic IoT2050 Advanced edge devices that a remote, unauthenticated attacker could use to execute code with elevated privileges. Also in the batch: an OS command injection in Siemens Siveillance Video / Milestone XProtect management servers (CVE-2026-3014, CVSS v3.1 9.1, v4.0 6.4) exploitable by users holding edit permissions, and two Siemens License Server flaws — CVE-2026-69108 (CVSS 6.0, local privilege escalation via an insecure sudoers policy) and CVE-2026-69109 (CVSS 7.5, path traversal), fixed in v5.1+ and v5.3+ respectively. Schneider Electric addressed two code/command execution issues in NetBotz 5 and an authentication-attempt flaw in PowerChute Serial Shutdown. Phoenix Contact published a PLCnext firmware advisory covering unauthenticated denial-of-service and malicious SQL query execution. - Siemens ProductCERT, Schneider Electric, Phoenix Contact — via SecurityWeek and CISA ICSA-26-225-07 / -09 - Vendor release 11 Aug 2026; reported 12–13 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] Coast Guard Cyber Command: maritime cyber incidents up 17%, and OT featured in 62% of its missions
item.description: The US Coast Guard Cyber Command’s fifth annual Cyber Trends and Insights in the Marine Environment report found reported maritime cyber incidents rose 17% year on year, and that operational technology featured in 62% of its cyber missions in 2025 against 46% the year before. Phishing remains the dominant initial-access vector. The command’s emphasis is deliberately unfashionable: multi-factor authentication, securing terminal operating systems, and having a tested incident-response plan matter more than advanced detection tooling for most operators in this sector. The OT percentage is the number to watch — it suggests the Coast Guard is increasingly finding control-system involvement in incidents that get reported as IT problems. - USCG Cyber Command annual report — via SAFETY4SEA - Published 8 Jul 2026

item.title: [Medium] Vessels are going dark on AIS in conflict waters — degrading the picture everyone else navigates by
item.description: Weekly maritime security reporting documented vessels withholding AIS broadcasts during a 4 August 2026 strike on Ukrainian port shipping, and a Saudi-flagged tanker not transmitting AIS when targeted by Houthi missiles on 5 August. Important distinction: this is deliberate signal suppression by mariners protecting themselves, not confirmed adversary spoofing. The security consequence is the same either way — the shared maritime picture that port authorities, VTS and collision-avoidance systems depend on degrades in exactly the areas where situational awareness matters most, and genuine spoofing becomes harder to distinguish from ordinary self-protective silence. Any detection logic that treats AIS gaps as inherently suspicious will drown in false positives in these waters. - Palaemon Maritime Security Report - Events 4–5 Aug 2026; reported 10 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Dragos counted 1,140 industrial ransomware incidents in Q2 — and not one reached stage 2 of the ICS kill chain
item.description: Dragos’s Q2 2026 industrial ransomware analysis recorded 1,140 incidents against industrial organisations, up 12% on Q1. Manufacturing absorbed 747 of them (65%), led by construction at 176 and equipment manufacturing at 114; food and beverage accounted for 70. The finding worth carrying into your own risk conversations is the negative one: Dragos found no case in Q2 where a ransomware operator reached stage 2 of the ICS Cyber Kill Chain. Production stopped because enterprise IT and ERP systems stopped — order entry, scheduling, shipping, labelling — not because anyone touched a controller. Named Q2 cases include West Pharmaceutical Services and Foxconn, the latter with a roughly two-week outage at Wisconsin and Texas sites. That pattern should shape where you spend: the loss is real, but the control is IT/OT dependency mapping and recovery, not deeper controller hardening. - Dragos Q2 2026 Industrial Ransomware Analysis — via Help Net Security - Published 10–11 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] MARAD’s standing advisory on Chinese-made cranes, LOGINK and scanners remains the operative US reference
item.description: MARAD advisory 2026-007 flags cyber risk from Chinese-manufactured ship-to-shore cranes (ZPMC), the LOGINK port-logistics data platform, and Nuctech security scanners, recommending network segmentation, multi-factor authentication and physical controls around crane systems. It was published in April 2026 and is included here as background rather than fresh news — it remains the current authoritative US government reference for a concern that has not gone away. No active exploitation of crane OT has been publicly confirmed. The practical value is the mitigation list, which is worth applying to any large, vendor-maintained, remotely-serviceable machine on your site regardless of where it was built. - US Maritime Administration advisory 2026-007 - Published 24 Apr 2026 — background, still current

item.title: [Info] Cyber Europe 2026 stress-tested rail and maritime operators together
item.description: ENISA ran what it described as its largest cybersecurity exercise to date on 10–11 June 2026, simulating coordinated attacks against European rail and maritime transport networks; Italy alone fielded 21 critical-infrastructure operators. Pairing the two sectors in one scenario is the interesting design choice — it reflects how a disruption to intermodal freight propagates across both, and how the two regulatory regimes (NIS2, the rail security directives, IACS class rules) intersect in practice. Exercise findings are not fully public, but participation is a reasonable proxy for maturity: operators who took part have a tested playbook and named the gaps, and those who did not have neither. - ENISA Cyber Europe 2026 — via Ports Europe - Exercise 10–11 Jun 2026; reported 17 Jun 2026
